result: Four novel bacteriophages (Clew-1, -3, -6, and -10) were isolated from wastewater that can form plaques on a ΔfliF ΔpilA double mutant of P. aeruginosa PAO1 but not on the wild-type strain. Subsequent testing determined that the fliF deletion (not pilA) rendered P. aeruginosa permissive for infection.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, with one stating the authors 'were able to isolate 4 new phages, CLEW-1, -3, -6 and -10, that were unable to infected the parental PAO1F Wt strain' and that 'the 4 phages were only able to infect a ΔfliF strain.' The editor describes the work as 'convincing' and the isolation approach as novel.

result: The Clew bacteriophages belong to the family of Bruynogheviruses and morphologically are Podoviruses, as determined by phylogenetic analysis and electron microscopy.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question the phylogenetic classification or morphological characterization. One reviewer summarizes the findings without critique, and the editor describes the work as 'convincing,' implicitly accepting these characterization claims.

result: Mutations affecting the MS-ring (ΔfliF) and associated proteins FliE or FliG resulted in Clew-1 sensitivity, while mutations in the ATPase complex conferred only partial sensitivity. Mutations affecting the hook, flagellar filament, or type III secretion function did not result in sensitivity, leading to the conclusion that the MS-ring presence controls phage sensitivity.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm this mechanistic finding. One reviewer states 'Through further mutational analysis of the flagellum apparatus, the authors were able to identify the involvement of c-di-GMP in phage infection' and notes the data 'strongly supports their conclusions.' No concerns are raised about the flagellar mutant analysis.

result: Clew-1 susceptibility is controlled by intracellular c-di-GMP levels. Deletion of fleQ had minor effects on wild-type susceptibility but decreased ΔfliF mutant susceptibility. Lowering c-di-GMP levels restored Clew-1 resistance in the ΔfliF2 mutant, while deleting wspF (elevating c-di-GMP) rendered wild-type bacteria phage sensitive, demonstrating that absence of the MS-ring controls susceptibility through increased c-di-GMP.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding. One states 'the authors were able to identify the involvement of c-di-GMP in phage infection' and notes 'Depletion of c-di-GMP levels by an inducible phosphodiesterase render the bacteria resistant to phage infection, while elevation of c-di-GMP through the Wsp system made the cells sensitive to infection by CLEW-1.' The data is described as strongly supporting conclusions.

result: TnSeq analysis in wild-type PAO1F infected with Clew-1 identified genes whose disruption led to phage sensitivity, including fliF, fliG, pch, and bifA. The depletion of pch and bifA insertions (both encoding c-di-GMP phosphodiesterases) further supports the role of c-di-GMP in controlling Clew-1 sensitivity.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the TnSeq findings. One reviewer states 'Using TnSeq, the authors were able to not only reaffirm the involvement of c-di-GMP in phage infection but also able to identify the exopolysaccharide PSL as a downstream target for CLEW-1.' The experiments are described as 'thoughtful and rational' with data that 'strongly supports their conclusions.'

result: TnSeq analysis in a ΔfliF mutant identified insertions in the psl operon as highly enriched after Clew-1 selection. Deletion of pslC or pslD rendered the ΔfliF mutant bacteria Clew-1 resistant, and sensitivity could be restored through complementation, demonstrating that Psl production is required for Clew-1 infection.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding. One states the TnSeq 'identified the exopolysaccharide PSL as a downstream target for CLEW-1' and notes 'deletion of the pslC gene resulted in complete phage resistance.' The editor describes the identification of Psl as a receptor as a key contribution of this 'valuable study.'

result: Attachment of phage Clew-1 is Psl-dependent in both wild-type and ΔfliF2 mutant bacteria, with a statistically significant increase in the percentage of bacteria with attached phage in the ΔfliF2 mutant. The ΔfliF2 mutant was lysed after ~40 min of infection, while wild-type bacteria showed growth slowing but not clear lysis. The increase in c-di-GMP in the ΔfliF2 mutant increases the fraction of Clew-1 susceptible cells in the population.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these attachment and lysis findings without critique. One reviewer notes 'The authors show that CLEW-1 binds directly to PSL on the cell surface' and describes the data as strongly supporting conclusions. The experiments are characterized as 'thoughtful and rational.'

result: Phage Clew-1 can be precipitated from culture supernatants using an anti-Psl antibody, with partially purified cell-associated Psl, and with biotinylated affinity-purified Psl, demonstrating that Clew-1 binds Psl directly.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm this direct binding evidence. One states 'The authors show that CLEW-1 binds directly to PSL on the cell surface' and the editor describes the work as 'convincing.' One reviewer notes that 'further characterisation of the CLEW-1 interaction with PSL at the molecular level would also have been welcomed' but treats this as future work rather than a weakness of the current claims.

result: Treatment of day-one biofilms with phage Clew-1 resulted in a statistically significant decrease in biofilm mass, while control phage Ocp-2 did not reduce biofilm. Clew-1 was not able to reduce biofilm formed by PA14 (a natural psl mutant). Clew-1 replicated on biofilm bacteria, reduced viable CFU, and increased the fraction of PI-positive (dead) cells in biofilms.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support the biofilm disruption findings. One states 'The authors also provide evidence that the phage - PSL interaction happens during the biofilm mode of growth and that the addition of the CLEW-1 phage specifically resulted in a significant loss of biofilm biomass.' The editor highlights that the phage can 'disrupt biofilms' as a key finding.

result: In a mouse model of P. aeruginosa keratitis (which involves biofilm formation), phage Clew-1 treatment significantly reduced bacterial burden and in some instances completely eradicated the infection. Corneal opacity was also reduced, indicating that inflammation was starting to resolve.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the in vivo efficacy findings. One reviewer notes 'the authors set out to test if CLEW-1 could be used to resolve a biofilm infection using a mouse keratitis model' and states 'the authors noted a reduction in bacterial load assessed by GFP fluorescence.' While the reviewer notes 'the keratitis did not resolve under the tested parameters,' this is presented as an observation rather than a critique of the claims about bacterial burden reduction.

result: Psl is not a capsular polysaccharide, distinguishing Clew phages from capsule-targeting phages like KP32. Unlike Klebsiella phages that use capsular depolymerase, Clew-1 has no such activity, indicating that the role of Psl in infection is distinct from capsule-targeting bacteriophage.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question this mechanistic distinction. The characterization is accepted as part of the overall 'convincing' work, and no concerns are raised about the lack of depolymerase activity or the comparison to capsule-targeting phages.

result: Phage Clew-1 fails to plaque on wild-type P. aeruginosa PAO1 but forms plaques on a fliF mutant. The fliF mutation generates a c-di-GMP-dependent signal that up-regulates Psl production and increases the fraction of bacteria to which the phage can bind. Plaque formation is likely masked in wild-type bacteria by the fraction of cells that are not phage-susceptible. This suggests Clew-1 has evolved to replicate in biofilm-growing P. aeruginosa, and standard isolation procedures likely exclude bacteriophage adapted to using biofilm markers.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this interpretation. One states the authors 'have not only developed a new technique for screening for phages targeting P. aeruginosa, but also highlights the importance of looking for phages during the biofilm mode of growth.' The editor describes this as a 'novel approach to control biofilms' and the work as 'valuable.'

result: Other biofilm-tropic bacteriophages have been described (including Knedl), suggesting more such phages await discovery. Using a ΔfliF ΔpilA double mutant will allow enrichment for biofilm-specific bacteriophage by excluding type IV pilus-dependent phage and up-regulating biofilm-specific surface structures. This isolation method can be extended to other bacterial species and will fuel discovery of biofilm-tropic bacteriophage.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the broader implications. One states the authors 'have not only developed a new technique for screening for phages targeting P. aeruginosa' and the approach 'highlights the importance of looking for phages during the biofilm mode of growth.' The editor describes the work as suggesting 'a novel approach to control biofilms.'

result: Biofilms formed by P. aeruginosa at infection sites significantly increase treatment difficulty due to reduced antibiotic penetration and increased persister bacteria. P. aeruginosa is a worrisome ESKAPE pathogen, and phage therapy has garnered interest as an alternative. Phage Clew-1 shows promise as a treatment modality since it killed biofilm bacteria in vitro and controlled P. aeruginosa infection in a mouse keratitis model.
evaluation: Reviewers support the therapeutic potential. The editor states the work 'suggests a novel approach to control biofilms that is relevant to researchers working on biofilms, specifically in Pseudomonas, on phage physiology and discovery, and on alternatives to controlling bacterial pathogens.' One reviewer notes the work is 'valuable' and the findings are 'convincing.'

result: Clew-1 plaques can sometimes look turbid, likely because Clew-1 can only bind to a fraction of the bacterial population (80-90% in PAO1 ΔfliF2). The inability to isolate Clew-1 lysogens is consistent with observations using other Bruynogheviruses and argues that Clew-1 is lytic and not temperate.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these observations about plaque morphology or lysogeny. The characterization is accepted as part of the overall 'convincing' work describing phage properties.

result: While many bacteriophages cannot infect P. aeruginosa biofilms, some biofilm-targeting phages have been described. Clew-1 does not require A- or B-band LPS for infection, but TnSeq identified genes involved in outer core LPS biosynthesis, and testing confirmed that ssg (PA5001) is required for Clew-1 infection.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question the LPS requirements or the identification of ssg. These findings are accepted as part of the mechanistic characterization, with one reviewer noting the experiments are 'thoughtful and rational' and data 'strongly supports their conclusions.'

result: While previous work noted that flagellar mutations lead to increased c-di-GMP and Psl production upon surface contact, the current results show phage susceptibility was primarily due to loss of the MS-ring and associated proteins (FliEFG), not the flagellar filament (FliC). TnSeq found insertions in flagellar genes, pch, and bifA resulted in Clew-1 sensitivity. Phages such as Clew-1 or Knedl could be useful tools for interrogating c-di-GMP signaling pathways in P. aeruginosa.
evaluation: Reviewers support these mechanistic insights. One states the authors 'were able to identify the involvement of c-di-GMP in phage infection' through 'mutational analysis of the flagellum apparatus.' The experiments are described as 'thoughtful and rational' with data that 'strongly supports their conclusions.'

result: Psl is a critical biofilm exopolysaccharide needed for surface attachment and structural stability. It has been detected on bacterial surfaces in helical patterns and is deposited by motile explorer bacteria. Psl interferes with immune functions and enhances bacterial survival. Clew-1 uses Psl as a receptor, infects only a subpopulation of planktonic P. aeruginosa, but can disrupt biofilms, replicate efficiently on biofilm-grown bacteria, and reduce bacterial burden in a corneal infection model involving biofilm formation.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this integrated finding. The editor states this 'valuable study identifies a novel bacteriophage that can use the exopolysaccharide Psl of Pseudomonas aeruginosa to infect and disrupt biofilms.' One reviewer notes the work 'identified a new bacteriophage that uses the exopolysaccharide Psl from Pseudomonas aeruginosa as a receptor' and the findings are 'convincing.'
